 The Complete November Social Security Payment Schedule
 Here's when your November check arrives and what could shift the usual timing.
 By
 Chris Lewis, CEPF 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Oct. 29, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
If you count on Social Security to cover rent, groceries, or medication costs, 
knowing exactly when your payment lands matters. The Social Security 
Administration doesn't send every check on the same day. Instead, it spreads 
payments across the month based on your birth date, whether you receive 
Supplemental Security Income (SSI), and when you first started collecting 
benefits. 
November brings its own quirks, including a federal holiday that falls on a day 
some beneficiaries typically get paid. Here's a full breakdown of when your 
money should arrive, how much the average retiree can expect, and what to do if 
a payment seems late. If you're stretching every check, there are also ways that 
could help 
 with bills if you're living on just Social Security .

 How the Social Security payment schedule works
The Social Security Administration (SSA) doesn't use a single payment date for 
everyone. Instead, it assigns payment days based on several factors: whether you receive SSI, when you began receiving Social Security, and the birth date associated with the earnings record on which you receive benefits. According to the SSA's published schedule, it breaks down like this: 
 Born 1st-10th: Paid on the second Wednesday of the 
 month
 Born 11th-20th: Paid on the third Wednesday of the 
 month
 Born 21st-31st: Paid on the fourth Wednesday of the 
 month
 SSI recipients: Generally paid on the 1st of the month
 Started receiving Social Security before May 1997, or receive both 
 Social Security and SSI: Paid on the 3rd of the month

 November's complete Social Security payment calendar
Here's how the dates line up for November 2026, based on the SSA's official 
payment calendar: 
 October 30, 2026 (Friday): SSI payment for November. Since 
 November 1 falls on a Sunday, the SSA issues this payment on the prior business 
 day.
 November 3, 2026 (Tuesday): Payment for beneficiaries who 
 started receiving Social Security before May 1997, and for those who receive 
 both Social Security and SSI.
 November 10, 2026 (Tuesday): Payment for beneficiaries born 
 on the 1st through the 10th, issued early because November 11 is Veterans Day. 
 November 18, 2026 (Wednesday): Third Wednesday payment for 
 those born on the 11th through the 20th.
 November 25, 2026 (Wednesday): Fourth Wednesday payment for 
 those born on the 21st through the 31st.
 What's different about November's schedule?
Two things stand out this month. First, because November 1 lands on a Sunday, 
SSI payments typically due on the 1st shift to the last business day of the 
prior month, which is October 30 this year. This is a standard SSA practice when 
a payment date falls on a weekend or federal holiday, not a special exception. 
Second, Veterans Day falls on Wednesday, November 11, the same day as the 
second-Wednesday payment for beneficiaries born on the 1st through the 10th. 
Because November 11 is a federal holiday, the SSA moves that payment up one day 
to Tuesday, November 10. The third- and fourth-Wednesday payments on November 18 
and 25 aren't affected. 
Social Security offices are also closed on Veterans Day, 
so you might want to check your payment details through your my Social Security 
account or the SSA's published calendar ahead of time.

 How much you can expect to receive
Benefit amounts vary widely based on lifetime earnings and the age someone 
starts claiming, but the SSA publishes regular averages that offer a useful 
benchmark. The SSA's 2026 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) fact sheet provides 
these estimated monthly averages for January 2026, after the 2.8% adjustment: 
 Average monthly benefit for all retired workers: 
 $2,071
 Average for an aged couple, both receiving benefits: 
 $3,208
 Average for a widowed mother with two children: $3,898
 Average for an aged widow or widower alone: $1,919
 Average for all disabled workers: $1,630
The maximum federal SSI payments for 2026 are: 
 Maximum federal SSI payment for an individual: $994 per 
 month
 Maximum federal SSI payment for a couple: $1,491 per 
 month
On the higher end, the SSA's maximum-benefit guidance shows that a worker who 
delays claiming until age 70 in 2026 could receive as much as $5,181 per month, 
under the SSA's stated earnings assumptions. That figure assumes the worker 
earned at or above the Social Security taxable maximum every year starting at 
age 22. The taxable maximum is $184,500 for 2026. 
Someone claiming at full 
retirement age in 2026 could receive up to $4,152 per month, while someone 
claiming at 62 could receive up to $2,969 per month. These examples apply to 
people starting benefits in 2026 under those assumptions, rather than 
representing a single maximum for everyone receiving retirement benefits. 
 How your benefit amount is calculated
The SSA calculates benefits using a formula based on your average indexed 
monthly earnings (AIME), which draws from up to 35 years of your highest-earning 
working years, adjusted for wage growth over time. That average feeds into a 
formula that produces your primary insurance amount (PIA), the benefit you'd 
receive if you claimed at your full retirement age (FRA). 
FRA is 67 for people born in 1960 or later. For workers who turn 62 in 2026, the 
PIA formula applies 90% to the first $1,286 of AIME, 32% to the amount above 
$1,286 through $7,749, and 15% to the amount above $7,749. These thresholds, 
known as bend points, depend on the worker's eligibility year, not simply the 
year a payment is received. 
Claiming before FRA permanently reduces your monthly benefit, while delaying 
past FRA, up to age 70, increases it through delayed retirement credits. The 
SSA's online Retirement Estimator could help you see how your own earnings 
history and claiming age could affect your personal benefit amount. 
 How to plan around your payment date
Knowing your specific payment date could help with budgeting, especially if 
bills or automatic payments are due around the same time each month. Some 
beneficiaries find it helpful to set up a short buffer between when Social 
Security arrives and when other bills are due, giving breathing room if a bank 
processing issue delays a payment. 
It may also help to confirm your payment method and direct deposit details 
through your my Social Security account periodically, especially after a bank 
change or a move. Beneficiaries who still receive paper checks may want to build 
in extra time for mail delivery. Federal benefits are moving to electronic 
payments, and the SSA plans to finish that switch for all beneficiaries in 2026.

 Bottom line
November's payment schedule follows the SSA's standard structure, with two 
adjustments. SSI payments shift to October 30 because November 1 falls on a 
Sunday, and the second-Wednesday payment moves to Tuesday, November 10, because 
of Veterans Day. Otherwise, the usual birth-date tiers apply for retirement and 
disability benefits paid later in the month. 
Beyond knowing your payment date, it's worth periodically checking your benefit 
amount and earnings record through your my Social Security account. Small 
discrepancies in your earnings history could affect your future benefit 
calculations, and catching them early is easier than correcting them after 
you've already claimed. 
And if your check doesn't go as far as you'd like, a few 
simple moves could help you stretch 
 your retirement dollars further .

 FAQs
 Can I change my Social Security payment date to better match my bills?
 No. The SSA assigns your payment date under its scheduling rules. If your bills consistently come due before your deposit arrives, consider asking your creditors or utility providers whether they can move your due dates.
 Does my November Social Security payment cover November or October?
 Social Security retirement and survivor benefits are generally paid one month behind, so a payment received in November covers October. SSI follows a different rule: It is paid for the current month, even when a calendar adjustment moves the deposit into the previous month.
 Why is my bank deposit smaller than my stated Social Security benefit?
 Your stated benefit may be the gross amount before deductions. Medicare Part B premiums are generally deducted from Social Security payments, which can make the amount deposited into your account lower. Review your benefit notice to see which deductions apply.
